items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I did get to know Charlie Parker in New York, but we were not great friends.

ctx.x: Monday was our night off, so all but the two local musicians would grab the first morning train for the Apple. I had a girl friend named Irene Henderson, and I would spend Mondays with her. The second Monday, we had free, and spent it the same as the first one. But when we arrived at our Hotel in Baltimore that Tuesday afternoon, Kirby told us that the job was finished. He didn't give us a plausible reason, and some of us pushed the matter because we were not very keen about the job from the first night we worked…

By this time, the Bebop movement was catching on, having started on 52nd Street with musicians like Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie. There were only a few big bands going, mostly playing theatres. The Ballrooms were still open but usually had small combos. Even the Savoy Ballroom was no longer a place which interested me. The atmosphere was no longer the same. Things were bad economically, and they were starting to tax the dance halls very heavily after the war. Also, Bebop was hard music to dance to, a fact…

The only interesting thing musically that happened for me on during the next few weeks was a concert/the 9th of June at the Town Hall. This concert was presented by my old friend Timmie Rosenkrantz, and the line up was another who's who inthe jazz world. Red Norvo had an orchestra composed of Joe (Flip) Phillips, Shorty Rodgers, Aaron Sachs, Eddie Bert, Remo Palmieri, Teddy Wilson and Slam Stewart. A fellow named Fran Warren did a voice and drum solo. Don Byas and Slam Stewart did a couple of duets. Erroll Garner…

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: if Charlier Parker and Miles Davis were one time members of Jay McShann's orchestra, I had the honour of having him accompany me.

ctx.x: It has been two years since I had not been in London again, but the occasion came for the Expo which was a week long festival, sponsored by the Harold Davison Agency and George Wain, that featured many American musicians as well as English groups, and once again, I was to meet and work with a famous musician I had heard and read plenty about but never seen.

This was the pianist Jay McShann, and his personality sent me as soon as we were introduced. He, Charles Shavers, Buddy Tate, Albert Nicholas and I, did a public aduience T.V.show for the B.B.C. at Ronnie Scott's club. Jay played and sang some real gone blues which knocked everybody out and when it came to accompanying me on my numbers, it was the first time I had been sent the way he sent me, in many moons. I have a tape of that session, thanks to an English jazz lover and friend of mine, named Leslie Parr, and…
There was a fine English bass man backing us up but the drummer was a little too modern and ligjt for our style.
